Many young people now buy second-hand clothes. They say it is cheaper and better for the planet. Others prefer new clothes because they last longer.

residents worry about traffic and noise

paper news is easier to trust

A2.passage: Some families do not give their children pocket money. They say children should earn it by helping at home. Others think every child needs a little money.

every child needs a little money

doctors find it hard to check patients

A2.passage: Some parents give young children a mobile phone. They can call home if there is a problem. Others think young children spend too much time on screens.
Many students work part-time while they study. They earn money and learn new skills. But some teachers say students become too tired to study well.

students get too tired to study

A2.passage: Our village will get fast internet next year. Young people are very happy. Some older people say the money is better spent on the bus service.
A popular music festival will come to our town this summer. Hotels and cafes will make money. But people who live nearby expect loud music until late.
key_points: hotels and cafes will make money

A2.passage: Some schools now finish lessons earlier on Fridays. Teachers have time for planning. Working parents find it hard to collect their children so early.
More people are choosing to rent a car only when they need one. It saves money on parking and repairs. Others say having your own car is easier.
Many supermarkets now sell ugly fruit and vegetables at lower prices. Shoppers save money and less food is wasted. Some people still prefer perfect-looking food.
Some airports now have quiet rooms where travellers can rest. Many people like this idea. Others say airports should spend money on more seats first.
Our town wants to plant trees along the main street. Trees give shade and clean air. Shop owners worry that the trees will hide their signs.

shop owners worry about hidden signs

A2.passage: Some gyms are now open all day and all night. People can exercise after work that finishes late. Others feel unsafe going to the gym alone at night.

key_points: cooking once saves time and money
eating the same food is boring

A2.passage: Some cafes do not allow laptops at weekends. They want people to talk and relax. Students who like to study there are not happy.

A2.passage: Many teenagers now learn to cook at school. They will eat better as adults. Some parents think schools should spend that time on maths and science.

A2.passage: A new road will go around our town. Lorries will not drive through the centre anymore. But the road will cut through farms and forest.

the road will cut through farms and forest

A2.passage: Some people now buy food for the whole month in one trip. It saves time and money. Others shop every few days because they want fresh food.
key_points: monthly shopping saves time and money

A2.passage: Our library now lends tools like drills and ladders. People do not need to buy expensive tools. Some shop owners say it hurts their business.
Many young people move to big cities for work. They find better jobs there. But rent is high, and they often miss their families.
Some offices now have no fixed desks. Workers sit in a different place every day. Some like meeting new colleagues, but others miss their own space.
Our town will close the main street to cars on Sundays. Families can walk and cycle safely. Some shop owners worry fewer customers will come.
key_points: main street closed to cars on Sundays

A2.passage: Some hotels no longer clean rooms every day. They say it saves water and energy. Some guests feel they are paying for less service.

guests feel they get less service

A2.passage: More people are using sharing apps to borrow things from their neighbours. It saves money and space. Some people worry their things will come back broken.
Some schools now teach children outside in the forest one day a week. The children love it. Some parents worry about cold weather and dirty clothes.
key_points: forest lessons one day a week
parents worry about cold and dirt

A2.passage: Our town museum will start charging for tickets next month. The money will pay for repairs. Some people say families with little money will stop visiting.
Many people now give gift cards instead of presents. They are easy to buy, and people can choose what they want. Others say gift cards feel less personal.
key_points: gift cards are easy and give choice

A2.passage: Some companies give workers a day off on their birthday. Workers feel happy and valued. Some managers say it is difficult when many people are away.
More people now walk with headphones on. They enjoy music or podcasts. But some drivers say these walkers do not hear cars coming.

B1.passage: Several universities have started recording all their lectures and putting them online. Students who miss a class can catch up easily. However, some lecturers worry that fewer students will turn up in person.
key_points: lectures are recorded and put online

B1.passage: A growing number of employers are offering unlimited holiday to their staff. Supporters say it shows trust and helps people avoid burnout. Critics point out that many workers take fewer days off when there is no fixed limit.
key_points: workers may take fewer days off

B1.passage: Some train companies have introduced quiet carriages where phone calls and loud music are not allowed. Many passengers welcome the peace. Others say the rules are hard to enforce and staff rarely check them.
key_points: quiet carriages ban calls and music

B1.passage: Many towns are turning empty shops into community spaces such as art studios and meeting rooms. Supporters say this brings life back to the high street. Others argue the buildings should be used for new businesses instead.
key_points: brings life to the high street

B1.passage: Some companies have stopped asking for university degrees when they hire new staff. They say skills and experience matter more. Others believe a degree still shows that a person can work hard and learn.

Several cities now charge tourists a small daily tax when they stay overnight. The money pays for cleaning and public services. Hotel owners, however, fear that visitors will choose cheaper places to stay.
key_points: tourist tax pays for cleaning and services

B1.passage: More secondary schools are banning mobile phones during the whole school day. Teachers report that students concentrate better and talk to each other more. Some parents, though, want to be able to contact their children in an emergency.

Many workplaces now hold short standing meetings instead of long seated ones. Supporters say people get to the point faster. Others feel that important topics are rushed and some staff never get a chance to speak.
Some airlines have started weighing passengers' hand luggage at the gate. They say it keeps flights on time and safe. Travellers complain that the rules are confusing and the extra fees are too high.
key_points: keeps flights on time and safe
rules are confusing and fees high

B1.passage: A number of councils are replacing grass in public areas with wild flowers. This helps bees and saves money on cutting. Some residents, however, think the areas look messy and attract insects.
More gyms are offering classes led by a screen instead of a real instructor. Prices have gone down as a result. But many members say they miss the personal advice and motivation of a trainer.
Some hospitals have begun sending patients home earlier and checking on them with home visits. This frees up beds for new patients. Critics worry that families end up doing too much of the care.

Several countries are considering raising the minimum driving age to eighteen. Supporters believe it would reduce accidents among young drivers. Others argue it would make life harder for teenagers in areas with poor public transport.
key_points: raising the driving age to eighteen
harder for teenagers with poor transport

B1.passage: Many restaurants now print the calories of every dish on their menus. Health experts say this helps people make better choices. Some diners feel it takes the fun out of eating out.
key_points: takes the fun out of eating out

B1.passage: A number of companies let employees choose their own job titles. Supporters say it makes people feel more creative and proud of their work. Critics say the titles confuse customers who do not know who to contact.
Some cities are building cycle lanes on busy roads by removing parking spaces. Cyclists feel much safer. Local shop owners, however, worry that customers who drive will no longer stop by.

Several schools have replaced written homework with reading time at home. Teachers say pupils feel less stressed and read more. Some parents are concerned that their children will fall behind in maths.
key_points: children may fall behind in maths

B1.passage: Many young people now choose apprenticeships instead of going to university. They earn money while they learn and avoid large debts. Others feel that a degree still opens more doors later in life.
key_points: apprenticeships let people earn while learning

B1.passage: Some supermarkets have removed sweets from the area near the checkouts. Parents say shopping with children is much easier now. Shop managers, though, report that sales of those products have dropped.

Some national parks now limit the number of visitors each day and ask people to book in advance. This protects nature and paths. However, many people feel that parks should be open to everyone freely.
key_points: parks limit visitors and need booking
parks should be open to all

B1.passage: Some theatres have started offering relaxed performances where audiences can move around and make noise. Families with young children welcome the change. Some regular theatre-goers say it spoils the experience for them.
key_points: regular audiences say it spoils the show

key_points: paid trial day before an offer
employed candidates cannot take a day off

B1.passage: Some cities have started switching off traffic lights at quiet junctions so that drivers must slow down and look carefully. Supporters say this reduces accidents. Others think it is confusing and dangerous for pedestrians.
key_points: drivers slow down and fewer accidents

B1.passage: Many apartment buildings now have shared laundry rooms instead of a washing machine in every flat. This saves space and energy. Some residents, however, dislike waiting for machines and sharing them with strangers.
key_points: shared laundry saves space and energy

B1.passage: A number of schools have introduced a later start time for teenagers, beginning lessons at ten o'clock. Research suggests teenagers learn better later in the day. However, parents who work early find the change difficult.
key_points: hard for parents who work early

B1.passage: More hotels are replacing front desk staff with machines where guests check themselves in. This is fast and cuts costs. Many guests, however, miss the friendly welcome and local advice from staff.
key_points: guests miss the welcome and advice

B1.passage: Some sports clubs have stopped keeping scores in games for children under ten. They want kids to enjoy playing without pressure. Some coaches argue that children need to learn how to win and lose.
key_points: children need to learn to win and lose

B1.passage: A number of cities are offering cash to people who move away from crowded centres to smaller towns. This can help small towns grow. Critics say it is expensive and few people actually move.
key_points: cash to move to small towns

B1.passage: Several companies now close their offices completely for two weeks in summer. Everyone takes a holiday at the same time, so no work piles up. Some staff dislike being told when to take their holiday.
Many concert venues now ask fans to lock their phones in small bags during shows. Artists say the audience enjoys the music more. Some fans are upset because they cannot take photos or videos.

Some local councils have started collecting rubbish every two weeks instead of every week. They say it saves money and encourages recycling. Residents complain about smells, especially in hot weather.
More people are taking 'gap years' to travel or work before starting university. Supporters say it helps them grow up and choose the right course. Others worry they will lose the habit of studying.
key_points: helps people grow and choose a course

B1.passage: Some banks now ask customers to answer extra security questions before every online payment. This helps stop fraud. However, many customers find the process slow and annoying, especially for small payments.
key_points: customers find them slow and annoying

B1.passage: Several cities have introduced free public transport for everyone. Car traffic has gone down in some places. But critics point out that someone still has to pay, usually through higher local taxes.

Many companies have started sending staff on volunteering days to help local charities. Employees enjoy doing something useful together. Some managers, however, complain about losing a full day of work.

B1.passage: Some primary schools have begun teaching children how to manage money, including saving and budgeting. Parents generally support the idea. Some teachers say the timetable is already too full to add another subject.
A number of beaches have banned smoking to keep the sand clean and protect children. Most visitors agree with the rule. Some smokers feel it goes too far, since beaches are open spaces.
key_points: keeps sand clean and protects children

B1.passage: More students are sharing flats with older people who have spare rooms, paying low rent in return for help around the house. Both sides can benefit. However, some people worry about privacy and different lifestyles.
key_points: students live with older people for low rent

B1.passage: Some film festivals now show new films online at the same time as in cinemas. More people can watch from home. Cinema owners worry this will reduce the number of tickets they sell.
key_points: films shown online and in cinemas

B1.passage: Several museums now allow visitors to take photos of the artworks. Visitors enjoy sharing their visit online. Others complain that crowds taking pictures make it hard to look at the art calmly.
key_points: crowds make it hard to enjoy the art

B2.passage: Facial recognition is increasingly being used at airports to speed up boarding. Supporters argue that queues are shorter and security is improved. Privacy groups, however, warn that travellers' data could be stored and misused if it is not properly protected.

Several governments are considering a tax on sugary snacks, similar to taxes already placed on soft drinks. Advocates claim it would reduce obesity and fund health services. Opponents argue it would hit low-income families hardest.
key_points: would reduce obesity and fund health

B2.passage: Many companies have begun publishing salary ranges in their job adverts. This is said to reduce pay gaps and save time for applicants. Some employers fear, however, that existing staff will demand raises if they discover newcomers earn more.
key_points: reduces pay gaps and saves time

B2.passage: Some universities are dropping entrance exams and selecting students based on school records and interviews instead. Supporters believe this gives talented students from weaker schools a fairer chance. Critics worry that standards will be harder to compare.
key_points: fairer for students from weaker schools

B2.passage: A growing number of cities are being redesigned so that residents can reach shops, schools and parks within a fifteen-minute walk. Supporters say this would cut traffic and strengthen communities. Critics fear it could restrict how freely people travel.

Lab-grown meat has been approved for sale in a few countries. Its supporters claim it could reduce animal suffering and greenhouse gases. Many consumers remain unconvinced, however, citing concerns about taste, price and how the product is made.
key_points: lab-grown meat approved in some countries
concerns about taste, price and production

B2.passage: Several airlines have been criticised for overbooking flights, a practice that assumes some passengers will not show up. Airlines argue it keeps fares lower. Passengers who are refused boarding, however, say that compensation rarely makes up for missed plans.
key_points: compensation does not cover missed plans

B2.passage: More employers are offering wellbeing programmes, such as meditation sessions and fitness allowances. These are intended to reduce stress and sick days. Critics argue that such programmes are no substitute for reasonable workloads and fair pay.
key_points: aim to reduce stress and sick days
no substitute for fair workloads and pay

B2.passage: Some schools have replaced traditional grades with written feedback. It is argued that students focus more on learning than on scores. However, universities and employers may find it harder to compare applicants if no grades are given.

Electric scooters can now be rented on the streets of many cities. They offer a cheap, low-emission way to travel short distances. Yet pedestrians frequently complain that scooters are ridden on pavements and left blocking paths.
key_points: rental e-scooters are cheap and clean

B2.passage: Some cities are introducing limits on how many cafes and restaurants can open in their historic centres. Supporters say this protects traditional shops and residents. Business owners argue that the market, not officials, should decide what opens.
key_points: limits on new cafes in historic centres

B2.passage: Many companies now track the location of delivery drivers throughout their shifts. Managers claim this improves efficiency and customer updates. Drivers, however, report feeling constantly watched and under pressure to meet unrealistic targets.

Some cities have introduced a ban on new fast-food outlets near schools. Health officials believe this would help reduce childhood obesity. Business owners argue that the rule is unfair and that families should be responsible for their own choices.
key_points: no new fast food near schools

B2.passage: Older buildings are often demolished to make way for modern housing. Developers argue that new homes are more energy-efficient and badly needed. Conservation groups insist that historic buildings should be preserved and adapted rather than replaced.
key_points: old buildings replaced by new housing
new homes are efficient and needed

B2.passage: Many hospitals now allow patients to read their own medical notes online. This is thought to improve understanding and trust. Some doctors worry, however, that patients could be alarmed by technical terms they do not fully understand.
key_points: patients can read their notes online

B2.passage: A number of countries are planning to ban the sale of new petrol cars within the next decade. Environmental groups welcome the deadline. Motorists and some manufacturers argue that charging networks will not be ready in time.
key_points: petrol car sales to be banned
charging networks may not be ready

B2.passage: Some companies have introduced 'no meeting' days to give staff uninterrupted time for focused work. Productivity is reported to have improved. However, some managers say important decisions are delayed when teams cannot meet.
key_points: no meeting days for focused work

B2.passage: Space tourism is expected to become more common as private flights grow cheaper. Enthusiasts say it could inspire interest in science. Critics point out that each flight produces large emissions while benefiting only the very wealthy.
key_points: high emissions for the wealthy few

B2.passage: Some cities have started fining residents who do not sort their rubbish correctly. Officials say recycling rates have risen significantly. Many residents feel the rules are too complicated and that fines are an unfair way to change behaviour.

A number of employers now allow staff to buy extra days of holiday through their salary. Employees value the flexibility. Some HR experts warn, however, that only better-paid staff can afford to take advantage of the scheme.
key_points: only better-paid staff can afford it

B2.passage: Smart meters are being installed in homes to show energy use in real time. Supporters say households will cut waste once they see their consumption. Critics doubt that the devices change behaviour and question how the data is used.
key_points: doubts about behaviour change and data use

B2.passage: Some sports leagues have introduced salary caps to limit how much clubs can spend on players. This is intended to keep competitions balanced. Critics argue that caps prevent the best players from being paid what they are worth.

Several cities have converted car lanes into bus-only lanes during rush hour. Bus journeys have become noticeably faster as a result. Drivers complain, however, that congestion has simply been pushed onto other roads.

Many large companies are now expected to report their carbon emissions each year. Investors argue this information is essential for making responsible decisions. Smaller firms fear the reporting requirements would be too costly for them.

More universities are offering degrees that can be completed entirely online. These programmes are cheaper and more flexible for working adults. However, some employers still doubt whether online graduates have received the same quality of education.

Some governments are considering limits on how many hours children can spend playing video games. Supporters argue this would protect sleep and mental health. Opponents insist that such decisions should be left to parents rather than the state.

Short-term holiday rentals have expanded rapidly in many popular cities. Homeowners can earn extra income, and tourists have more choice. Residents, however, complain that rents have risen and that neighbourhoods are losing their sense of community.

A growing number of supermarkets are being designed without any cashiers at all, with payments taken automatically as shoppers leave. Supporters praise the speed and convenience. Critics worry about job losses and the amount of personal data collected.

Some employers are offering financial rewards to staff who cycle or walk to work. This is believed to improve health and reduce parking demand. Others argue it is unfair to employees who live too far away to do so.
key_points: rewards for cycling or walking to work
unfair to those who live far away

B2.passage: In certain regions, new homes are required to be built with solar panels. Supporters say this would reduce energy bills over time. Builders argue that the extra costs will be passed on to buyers, making homes less affordable.
key_points: new homes must have solar panels

B2.passage: Some schools have adopted year-round calendars with shorter, more frequent holidays instead of one long summer break. Teachers say students forget less. Parents, however, find it harder to arrange childcare and family trips.

Cash machines are being removed from many rural areas as fewer people withdraw money. Banks say the machines are no longer cost-effective. Older residents and small businesses, however, claim they are being left without access to cash.
key_points: cash machines removed in rural areas
older people and businesses lose access

B2.passage: Some companies have started using virtual reality to train new staff in dangerous tasks. It is claimed that mistakes can be made safely and skills learned faster. However, the equipment is expensive, and some employees feel uncomfortable using it.

Several countries now offer special visas that allow foreigners to live there while working remotely for overseas employers. These visas bring spending into local economies. Critics argue that they push up housing costs for local people.

A number of cities are planting greenery on rooftops and walls to cool buildings during heatwaves. Supporters say green walls also improve air quality. Critics point out that maintenance costs are high and the benefits are difficult to measure.
key_points: green roofs and walls cool buildings

B2.passage: Many companies now run anonymous staff surveys to measure employee satisfaction. Managers say honest feedback would be impossible otherwise. Some employees doubt their answers are truly anonymous and suspect that little changes afterwards.

Professional sports referees are increasingly supported by video replay technology. Decisions are believed to be more accurate as a result. Many fans, however, complain that games are interrupted too often and lose their natural flow.

Several airports have introduced fees for dropping off passengers outside the terminal. Airport operators claim this reduces congestion and encourages the use of public transport. Travellers argue that it is simply another way of making money from them.
key_points: less congestion and more public transport
just a way to make money

B2.passage: Some publishers now release books in short weekly episodes on mobile apps. This attracts younger readers who prefer short sessions. Traditional authors fear, however, that stories will be written for quick clicks rather than quality.

Increasingly, job applicants are being asked to record video answers to interview questions. Recruiters say this speeds up hiring considerably. Candidates, however, often find it awkward to speak to a camera without any human reaction.

Many countries are raising the retirement age as people live longer. Governments argue that pension systems would otherwise become unaffordable. Workers in physically demanding jobs, however, say they cannot realistically work for several more years.

C1.passage: The widespread adoption of open-plan offices was intended to foster collaboration and break down hierarchies. Proponents maintain that spontaneous conversations spark ideas that would never arise behind closed doors. Yet a growing body of research suggests that constant noise and visibility drive employees to communicate less face to face, relying instead on messages and headphones.
key_points: open-plan offices meant to boost collaboration

C1.passage: Many universities have begun to place their course materials under open licences, allowing anyone to use and adapt them free of charge. Advocates argue that this widens access to knowledge and reduces textbook costs. Sceptics, however, question who will fund the work of creating and updating high-quality materials if they generate no revenue.

Platform-based work has given millions of people the flexibility to choose when and how much they work. Defenders of the model argue that this autonomy is precisely what many workers value. Critics counter that classifying these workers as self-employed deprives them of sick pay, pensions and protection against sudden loss of income.
key_points: no sick pay, pensions or income protection

C1.passage: Several historic cities have responded to overtourism by capping visitor numbers, restricting cruise ships and raising tourist taxes. Supporters contend that such measures are essential to preserve heritage sites and residents' quality of life. Opponents warn that businesses dependent on tourism could suffer and that culture risks becoming a privilege for the wealthy.
key_points: cities limit tourists and cruise ships
hurts tourism businesses and limits access

C1.passage: The routine use of antibiotics in livestock farming has helped producers keep animals healthy and food prices low. However, public health experts warn that it accelerates the emergence of drug-resistant bacteria, which threaten the effectiveness of treatments for humans. Farmers' associations argue that an outright ban would raise costs and compromise animal welfare.
key_points: antibiotics keep animals healthy and food cheap
a ban would raise costs and harm welfare

C1.passage: Linking teachers' pay to their students' exam results has been proposed as a way of rewarding excellence and raising standards. Supporters believe it would motivate staff and attract talented graduates. Critics argue that results depend heavily on factors beyond a teacher's control, and that such schemes encourage teaching to the test rather than genuine learning.

Many companies now offer customers the option of offsetting their emissions by funding tree-planting or renewable energy projects. Supporters regard offsets as a practical step while cleaner technology is developed. Critics, however, contend that they allow polluters to buy a clear conscience, and that the benefits of many projects are exaggerated or difficult to verify.
key_points: lets polluters buy a clear conscience

C1.passage: Generative writing tools are being adopted rapidly in offices to draft reports, emails and summaries. Proponents claim that they free professionals from routine tasks and allow them to concentrate on judgement and strategy. Others caution that over-reliance may erode writing skills, and that errors produced by the tools are easily overlooked by busy staff.
key_points: AI writing tools used in offices

C1.passage: Rewilding projects, which reintroduce native species and allow land to return to its natural state, have gained considerable public support. Ecologists argue that they restore biodiversity and help ecosystems cope with climate change. Farmers and rural communities, however, often feel excluded from decisions and fear losses to livestock and agricultural income.
key_points: farmers feel excluded and fear losses

C1.passage: Open-access publishing has made research freely available to anyone with an internet connection, rather than only to subscribers. While this is widely welcomed, the costs have often shifted to authors, who must pay substantial fees to publish. Researchers at less wealthy institutions argue that this simply replaces one barrier with another.
key_points: a new barrier for poorer institutions

C1.passage: Some employers now offer staff wearable fitness trackers, rewarding those who meet activity targets with lower insurance premiums. Advocates claim the schemes encourage healthier habits and reduce absence. Privacy specialists warn, however, that health data collected in the workplace could eventually influence decisions about promotion or dismissal.

Unpaid internships remain common in competitive sectors such as media, fashion and law. Employers argue that they offer valuable experience to young people who might otherwise struggle to get a foot in the door. Critics maintain that they favour those whose families can support them, thereby reinforcing existing inequalities in access to prestigious careers.

Smart city initiatives use sensors and data analysis to manage traffic, lighting and waste collection more efficiently. Municipal leaders highlight the potential savings and environmental benefits. Civil liberties groups, however, are concerned that the same infrastructure enables an unprecedented degree of monitoring, often without residents being consulted or informed.

Average grades at many universities have risen steadily over recent decades. Some academics attribute this to improved teaching and better-prepared students. Others suspect grade inflation, driven partly by institutions competing for fee-paying students, and warn that employers can no longer distinguish genuinely outstanding graduates from merely competent ones.
key_points: grade inflation makes graduates hard to tell apart

C1.passage: As countries seek to cut emissions, nuclear power has returned to the policy agenda. Supporters emphasise that it provides reliable, low-carbon electricity regardless of the weather. Opponents point to high construction costs, lengthy delays and the unresolved question of how radioactive waste should be stored safely for thousands of years.
key_points: nuclear power is back on the agenda
high costs, delays and waste storage

C1.passage: The rapid expansion of data centres has brought investment and jobs to many regions. Yet these facilities consume vast quantities of electricity and water for cooling. Local communities, particularly in areas prone to drought, increasingly question whether the economic benefits outweigh the strain on shared resources.
key_points: data centres bring investment and jobs
use huge amounts of power and water

C1.passage: Retail loyalty schemes reward customers with discounts and personalised offers. Behind the scenes, however, they gather detailed records of purchasing habits that are analysed and sometimes shared with third parties. Retailers maintain that customers knowingly exchange data for savings, while consumer groups argue that few people understand what they are giving away.
key_points: they collect and share shopping data
customers may not understand the trade

C1.passage: Desalination plants, which turn seawater into drinking water, are increasingly seen as a solution to water shortages in dry coastal regions. Supporters stress that they offer a supply independent of rainfall. Environmentalists, however, highlight their heavy energy demands and the damage that discharged salty waste can inflict on marine ecosystems.
key_points: desalination turns seawater into drinking water
high energy use and harm to sea life

C1.passage: Many minority languages are disappearing as younger generations adopt more widely spoken ones for education and employment. Some argue that governments should invest heavily in teaching and broadcasting in these languages to preserve cultural heritage. Others contend that limited public funds are better spent equipping young people with languages that improve their economic prospects.
key_points: funds better spent on useful languages

C1.passage: Some governments are considering compulsory labels showing the environmental footprint of food products. Proponents argue that shoppers cannot make informed choices without such information. Producers counter that calculating a reliable footprint is extremely complex, and that simplified scores could mislead consumers and penalise small farms.
key_points: complex to calculate and could mislead

C1.passage: Publishing performance rankings for hospitals is intended to increase transparency and drive improvement, allowing patients, in theory, to choose the best providers. Critics argue, however, that such tables reward hospitals that avoid complex cases, since treating the sickest patients inevitably produces worse outcomes on paper.

Several countries are moving rapidly towards becoming cashless, with most transactions now made by card or phone. Advocates point to lower handling costs and reduced tax evasion. Critics caution that elderly people, those without bank accounts and anyone in rural areas with poor connectivity risk being excluded from everyday economic life.
key_points: lower costs and less tax evasion
elderly, unbanked and rural people excluded

C1.passage: A number of high-profile studies in psychology and medicine have failed to produce the same results when repeated by other researchers. Some see this as evidence of a crisis in scientific practice, fuelled by pressure to publish surprising findings. Others argue that failed replications are simply part of how science corrects itself over time.
key_points: seen as a crisis driven by publishing pressure

C1.passage: Vertical farms grow crops indoors in stacked layers, using a fraction of the water and land required by conventional agriculture. Investors see them as a way to produce fresh food close to cities. Sceptics point out that their energy costs are considerable, and that only a narrow range of crops can be grown profitably.
key_points: vertical farms use little water and land
high energy costs and few profitable crops

C1.passage: The fast fashion industry has made stylish clothing affordable to a far wider public than ever before. However, its business model depends on rapid turnover, low wages in producing countries and enormous quantities of textile waste. Some campaigners call for strict regulation, while others believe informed consumers should drive change through their purchasing decisions.
key_points: relies on low wages and creates waste

C1.passage: Autonomous vehicles promise to reduce accidents caused by human error, which account for the vast majority of road collisions. Nevertheless, significant questions remain unresolved, particularly regarding who should be held liable when a driverless car causes harm. Insurers, manufacturers and legislators have yet to reach a consensus, leaving the public understandably wary.
key_points: no consensus and public is wary

C1.passage: Major museums increasingly rely on blockbuster exhibitions, heavily promoted and expensive to attend, to attract visitors and sponsorship. Directors argue that such events subsidise less popular but scholarly work. Critics complain that curatorial decisions are being driven by marketing considerations, and that permanent collections receive less attention and investment as a result.

Home genetic testing kits allow people to learn about their ancestry and potential health risks without visiting a doctor. Supporters view this as empowering individuals to take charge of their health. Medical professionals caution that results are often misinterpreted without expert guidance, and that sensitive genetic information may be stored by companies indefinitely.
key_points: home genetic tests show ancestry and risks

C1.passage: Offshore wind farms are expanding rapidly as governments pursue ambitious renewable energy targets. Their supporters stress that they generate substantial power without consuming land. Coastal communities and fishing industries, however, have raised concerns about the visual impact on seascapes and potential disruption to fishing grounds and marine wildlife.
key_points: lots of power without using land
concerns about views, fishing and wildlife

C1.passage: In several countries, the cost of university tuition has been shifted largely from the state to students through loans. Advocates argue that graduates, who tend to earn more, should contribute to the cost of their education. Opponents counter that large debts deter students from poorer backgrounds and distort career choices towards higher-paid professions.
key_points: graduates earn more so should pay
debt deters poorer students and distorts careers

C1.passage: As hybrid working becomes the norm, concerns have been raised about the development of junior staff. Senior employees value the autonomy of working from home, yet newcomers often learn by observing experienced colleagues. Some firms now require younger staff to attend the office more often, a policy that others consider inequitable.
key_points: concern for junior staff in hybrid work
requiring juniors in the office seen as unfair

C1.passage: Bans on single-use plastic packaging are popular with the public and have visibly reduced litter. However, some food scientists point out that plastic often extends the shelf life of fresh produce, and that removing it may increase food waste, potentially producing a greater environmental cost than the packaging itself.

Hosting major international sporting events is often promoted as a way to boost tourism, regenerate neglected areas and enhance national prestige. Economists, however, frequently find that the costs far exceed the benefits, leaving host cities with debts and underused stadiums. Supporters maintain that intangible benefits, such as civic pride, are difficult to quantify.
key_points: hosting events promises tourism and renewal
civic pride is hard to measure

C1.passage: News is increasingly delivered through personalised feeds that select stories based on users' previous behaviour. Supporters argue that this helps people find content relevant to their interests. Critics contend that it narrows exposure to differing viewpoints and rewards sensational material, gradually weakening the shared understanding on which public debate depends.

A growing number of patients travel abroad for surgery and dental treatment that would be costly or subject to long waiting lists at home. For many, the savings are substantial. Medical bodies, however, warn that complications can be difficult to manage once patients return, and that standards of care vary considerably between providers.

Increasingly accurate translation software has led some to question whether learning a foreign language remains worthwhile. Enthusiasts suggest that technology will soon remove most language barriers. Educators argue, however, that learning a language develops cognitive skills and cultural understanding that no device can replicate, and that machine output still misses nuance.
key_points: learning builds skills machines cannot replace

C1.passage: Some organisations now offer long-serving employees paid sabbaticals of several months to pursue study, travel or personal projects. Advocates claim that staff return refreshed and more committed, reducing turnover. Critics note that the policy is costly, difficult for small teams to absorb, and rarely available to those in junior or temporary roles.
key_points: costly and not for junior staff

C1.passage: Urban beekeeping has become fashionable, with hives appearing on office roofs and in city gardens. While it is promoted as a way to support declining pollinators, some ecologists argue that large numbers of honeybees compete with wild bees for limited flowers, potentially harming the very species the trend claims to protect.

A frequent flyer levy, under which the tax on air tickets rises with each additional flight a person takes in a year, has been proposed as a fairer way to reduce aviation emissions. Supporters note that a small minority take most flights. Opponents argue that it penalises those whose work or family ties require regular travel.
key_points: unfair to those who must travel

C1.passage: Educational apps increasingly use points, badges and leaderboards to keep learners engaged. Proponents argue that such features make practice more motivating, particularly for younger students. Researchers caution, however, that rewards can shift attention from understanding to collecting points, and that motivation often fades once the novelty wears off.
key_points: focus shifts to points and motivation fades

C1.passage: Local authorities often commission public art for new developments, arguing that it enhances shared spaces and gives neighbourhoods a distinct identity. Critics, however, regard such spending as a luxury when essential services face cuts, and residents are sometimes dismayed by works they had no say in choosing.
key_points: a luxury amid cuts and residents not consulted

C2.passage: The fetishisation of productivity metrics in knowledge work, ostensibly a route to accountability, has drawn mounting scepticism. Its advocates insist that what goes unmeasured goes unmanaged; detractors counter that the most valuable intellectual labour is precisely that which resists quantification, and that metrics inevitably distort the behaviour they purport to capture.

Proponents of nudge policies maintain that subtly redesigning choices, such as automatically enrolling employees in pension schemes, achieves socially desirable outcomes without curtailing liberty. Critics are less sanguine, contending that such interventions are paternalistic, bypass reasoned deliberation, and may erode citizens' capacity to make genuinely autonomous decisions.

Heritage restoration poses an enduring dilemma: should a damaged monument be returned to its presumed original state or bear the marks of its history? Purists regard reconstruction as a kind of forgery; others argue that sympathetic restoration alone lets the public grasp what was lost.
key_points: restore monuments or keep their history

C2.passage: The proliferation of credentials, from micro-certificates to postgraduate diplomas, has been hailed as a democratisation of learning. Yet sceptics discern a self-perpetuating arms race in which qualifications lose value as they multiply, compelling individuals to accumulate ever more expensive proof of competence merely to remain eligible for the same positions.
key_points: people pay more for the same jobs

C2.passage: Meritocracy, long regarded as the fairest principle for allocating opportunity, has recently attracted searching criticism. Detractors argue that it lends the successful an unwarranted sense of moral entitlement while stigmatising those left behind. Its defenders retort that the alternatives, patronage or inheritance, are demonstrably worse.

The museum's role as a neutral custodian of culture is increasingly contested. Some curators argue that institutions should engage explicitly with contemporary social questions, lest they become irrelevant. Others fear that overt advocacy compromises scholarly integrity and alienates visitors who expect a space for contemplation rather than instruction.
key_points: engage with social questions to stay relevant
advocacy harms integrity and alienates visitors

C2.passage: Proposals to price road use according to distance travelled, rather than taxing fuel, have gained traction as electric vehicles erode fuel revenues. Economists commend the elegance of charging for actual usage; privacy advocates, however, balk at the prospect of authorities tracking every journey, however benign the stated intention.
key_points: charging by distance instead of fuel tax

C2.passage: The ascendancy of English as the lingua franca of academic publishing has undeniably facilitated international collaboration. Nevertheless, scholars writing in other languages contend that it marginalises locally grounded research, privileges native speakers in peer review, and gradually impoverishes the conceptual vocabulary available within their own disciplines.
key_points: marginalises local research and other languages

C2.passage: Planned obsolescence, whether engineered deliberately or arising from incompatible software updates, has become a lightning rod for consumer frustration. Manufacturers insist that rapid innovation inevitably renders older devices outdated. Critics retort that the practice externalises environmental costs onto society while sustaining a lucrative cycle of replacement.
key_points: critics cite environmental costs and profit

C2.passage: Longtermism, the view that safeguarding the distant future should be a moral priority, has gained influence among philanthropists. Its adherents argue that the sheer number of potential future lives dwarfs present concerns. Sceptics counter that such reasoning is speculative and conveniently justifies neglecting tangible suffering in the present.

The gamification of personal finance, whereby investment apps borrow the visual language of games, has drawn a younger cohort into the markets. Enthusiasts welcome this broadening of participation; regulators, however, fret that confetti animations and streaks encourage impulsive trading, blurring the boundary between investing and gambling.

The quantified self movement, in which individuals meticulously log sleep, diet and mood, is lauded by its adherents as a path to self-knowledge. Detractors, though, suspect that perpetual self-surveillance breeds anxiety rather than insight, and that the data rarely prompts the behavioural change its devotees anticipate.
key_points: people track sleep, diet and mood
breeds anxiety and rarely changes behaviour

C2.passage: Governments routinely subsidise agricultural producers, citing food security and the preservation of rural landscapes. Economists object that such payments disproportionately benefit large landholders, inflate land prices and shield inefficient practices from competition, whereas defenders insist that farming's strategic importance justifies exemption from pure market logic.
key_points: farm subsidies for food security and landscapes

C2.passage: The notion of a work-life balance presupposes that the two can be neatly separated, an assumption that hybrid working has rendered increasingly tenuous. Some welcome the resulting integration as liberating; others contend that it has merely enabled employers to colonise previously protected hours.
key_points: hybrid work blurs work and life

C2.passage: Cultural institutions increasingly accept sponsorship from corporations whose activities sit uneasily with their stated missions. Pragmatists argue that without such funding, exhibitions and free admission would be unsustainable. Critics maintain that the arrangement confers reputational legitimacy on sponsors and subtly constrains what institutions are willing to display.
key_points: gives sponsors legitimacy and limits content

C2.passage: Geoengineering, the deliberate large-scale manipulation of the climate, was once dismissed as fanciful. As emissions targets slip, some scientists argue that researching techniques such as reflecting sunlight is a prudent precaution. Opponents fear that merely contemplating such options will weaken the resolve to cut emissions at source.
key_points: may weaken efforts to cut emissions

C2.passage: Antitrust regulators have traditionally judged mergers by their effect on consumer prices. With digital services often offered free of charge, some scholars argue that this framework is obsolete and that regulators should weigh effects on innovation and data concentration; others caution against stretching the law beyond workable boundaries.
key_points: free digital services make this outdated

C2.passage: Travellers increasingly prize authentic encounters with local life over conventional sightseeing. Anthropologists observe, however, that this very demand tends to generate staged performances of tradition. Some regard such commodification as corrosive; others argue that communities themselves often adapt their customs knowingly and profitably.

Credit scoring based on alternative data such as rental payments and phone bills promises to extend borrowing to those with thin credit histories. Proponents tout its inclusivity; critics warn that opaque models may encode existing disparities and penalise applicants for circumstances wholly unrelated to their reliability.
key_points: credit scores using rent and phone bills

C2.passage: Literary prizes are often credited with elevating neglected writers and sustaining public interest in serious fiction. Sceptics, however, regard them as arbitrary arbiters of taste whose verdicts reflect the preoccupations of small, insular juries, and whose commercial influence concentrates sales on a handful of titles.
key_points: prizes elevate writers and serious fiction

C2.passage: The expansion of compulsory schooling into early childhood is often justified by research showing lasting benefits from high-quality preschool education. Critics question whether such findings generalise to large public programmes, and some argue that formalised learning at so young an age displaces the unstructured play through which children develop.
key_points: may not scale and displaces play

C2.passage: Urban densification is championed by planners as a remedy for sprawl, congestion and housing shortages. Residents of established neighbourhoods, though, frequently resist taller buildings, citing strain on infrastructure and loss of character. Their opponents dismiss such objections as thinly veiled efforts to protect property values at newcomers' expense.
key_points: density fixes sprawl and housing shortages

C2.passage: Citizen assemblies, in which randomly selected members of the public deliberate on contentious policy questions, are hailed as an antidote to polarisation. Sceptics doubt whether laypeople can master complex technical issues in a matter of weekends, and question the legitimacy of bodies that answer to no electorate.

The vogue for 'disruption' has made incremental improvement seem unfashionable. Yet historians of technology note that most transformative innovations emerged through gradual refinement rather than sudden rupture. Champions of disruption retort that complacent incumbents seldom reform without the existential threat posed by insurgent competitors.
key_points: incumbents need the threat of disruption

C2.passage: Lifelong learning is routinely invoked as the answer to technological upheaval in the labour market. Critics observe, however, that the rhetoric conveniently transfers responsibility for adaptation from employers and governments onto individuals, many of whom lack the time, money or institutional support to retrain repeatedly.
key_points: lifelong learning as answer to job change
many lack time, money or support

C2.passage: Digital archives promise to preserve the cultural record indefinitely, yet archivists warn of a looming 'digital dark age': file formats become unreadable, platforms vanish, and links decay. Some advocate rigorous standards and redundancy; others contend that selective forgetting has always been integral to how societies construct memory.

The meteoric rise of wellness culture has encouraged people to take greater responsibility for their health. Detractors, however, argue that it often repackages unproven remedies as self-care, and that its emphasis on individual habits obscures the structural determinants of illness, such as poverty and working conditions.

Ethical consumption presumes that purchasing decisions can steer corporate behaviour. Sceptics contend that such individualised responses are largely symbolic, diverting energy from collective action and regulation. Its defenders reply that aggregated consumer choices have demonstrably transformed industries, from fair-trade coffee to free-range eggs.
key_points: largely symbolic and distracts from regulation

C2.passage: Microcredit was once celebrated as a panacea for poverty, enabling entrepreneurs without collateral to borrow modest sums. Subsequent evaluations have tempered that enthusiasm, finding modest effects on household income and occasional over-indebtedness. Advocates maintain that access to credit nonetheless expands borrowers' options and resilience.
key_points: microcredit was seen as a cure for poverty
studies show modest effects and debt

C2.passage: The practice of awarding contracts to the lowest bidder is defended as a safeguard of public money. Procurement specialists increasingly argue, however, that it incentivises unrealistic tenders, culminating in cost overruns and diminished quality, and that evaluating long-term value, though harder to audit, would ultimately prove more economical.
key_points: leads to overruns and poor quality

C2.passage: Expert consensus carries considerable weight in policy debates, yet history offers numerous examples of consensus later overturned. Some infer that dissenting voices deserve greater institutional protection; others caution that granting fringe views equal standing confuses the public and lends unwarranted credibility to positions with scant evidential support.

The aesthetics of minimalism, extolled as a liberation from material excess, has itself become a lucrative market. Critics observe the irony of consumers purchasing costly, carefully curated objects in pursuit of simplicity, while admirers insist that the underlying ethos of deliberate consumption remains valuable regardless of its commercial appropriation.

Sports analytics has transformed recruitment and tactics, replacing intuition with statistical modelling. Purists lament that the game has become formulaic and that scouts' tacit expertise is undervalued. Proponents counter that data merely exposes the biases and blind spots that unexamined intuition had long concealed.

Inheritance taxes are defended as a means of curbing entrenched privilege and promoting equality of opportunity. Opponents depict them as a double imposition on wealth already taxed, and argue that they penalise thrift and the natural desire to provide for one's descendants.

Literary translation inevitably entails compromise between fidelity to the original wording and fidelity to its spirit. Literalists contend that translators who take liberties usurp the author's voice; others maintain that a slavishly literal rendering betrays the work more profoundly by sacrificing rhythm, idiom and emotional resonance.
key_points: literal versions lose rhythm and feeling

C2.passage: Smart contracts, self-executing agreements encoded in software, promise to eliminate intermediaries and the ambiguities of legal language. Lawyers remain sceptical, observing that commercial relationships depend on discretion and good-faith interpretation in unforeseen circumstances, precisely the flexibility that rigid code is ill-equipped to provide.

Zoos have reinvented themselves as centres of conservation and education, citing breeding programmes for endangered species. Critics remain unconvinced, arguing that few captive-bred animals are ever reintroduced to the wild and that confining intelligent, wide-ranging creatures is ethically indefensible whatever the educational rationale.
key_points: few animals return to the wild

C2.passage: The biannual practice of changing the clocks, originally justified by energy savings, persists largely through inertia. Sleep researchers argue that the disruption carries measurable health costs, whereas opponents of abolition note the persistent disagreement over whether permanent summer or winter time would serve the public better.

The romanticisation of entrepreneurship portrays founders as heroic risk-takers whose success reflects vision and grit. Sociologists point out that a safety net of family wealth often underwrites such risk, and that survivorship bias renders the countless failures invisible, distorting aspiring founders' perception of their own prospects.

Intellectual property protection is defended as the indispensable incentive for creative and scientific endeavour. Yet critics contend that ever-lengthening copyright terms serve corporate rights-holders far more than living creators, and that excessively broad patents can stifle precisely the cumulative innovation they purport to encourage.

Volunteer tourism, in which travellers pay to work on development projects abroad, is marketed as mutually beneficial. Critics argue that short-term, unskilled volunteers may displace local workers and that the experience primarily serves participants' self-image; proponents counter that it fosters enduring global awareness.
key_points: may displace local workers and serve self-image
